results.title: Weighting | European Social Survey
results.content: ## Survey weights in the ESS. When analysing ESS data estimates, the likelihood of each respondent to be part of the sample should also be taken into account - which means that the most accurate estimates will be obtained only after weighting the data. For more information on how to use weights on ESS data consult the ESS weighting guide before conducting any analysis of ESS data. Four weighting variables are available: **Analysis weight** *(anweight - combination of pspwght and pweight)*, **Post-stratification weight** (*pspwght*), **Design weight** (*dweight*), and **Population weight** *(pweight)*. Anweight corrects for differential selection probabilities within each country as specified by sample design, for nonresponse, for noncoverage, and for sampling error related to the four post-stratification variables, and takes into account differences in population size across countries. The post-stratification weights are obtained by adjusting the design weights in such a way that they will replicate the distribution of the cross-classification of age group, gender, and education in the population and the marginal distribution for region in the population.

results.content: # Is data weighting necessary even if a stratified sample has been applied? In addition, data weighting has been applied on the collected data, with the objective to compensate non-respondents bias; weighting variables have been gender and area type again, as well as age group and education level. Is it correct to apply both pre-stratification and post data weighting? This can be done when the data collection is done when the participants were stratified before the beginning of the study (such as in an randomized design) or when stratification was done in the data after collection of the data (such as in an observational study). This can be done when the data collection is done when the participants were stratified before the beginning of the study (such as in an randomized design) or when stratification was done in the data after collection of the data (such as in an observational study). You only need to weight if there is any imbalance in sample profiles and it is done after data collection :). We can call "pre-stratified" as "stratified" where stratification process is done before data collection. There is also post-stratification, which is done after the data collection, as a special case. Data weighting can be done to adjust design weights, nonresponse, and post-stratification weights. My fixed effects are: Group (5 levels), Condition (2 levels), GenderS (gender of the speaker), GenderP (gender of the participant) and the interaction between all of those. Each participant rated 100 audio files (40 in the baseline condition and 60 in the experimental condition) giving a total of 8000 data points (1600 in each group). However, when I do the pairwise post hoc test with glth() and Holm's adjustment for only the Group:Condition interaction I get a non-significant effect. Now, I understand that ANOVA and post hoc answers two different questions. I have 5 groups and I was originally interested in the differences between those groups (in the experimental condition) so the Group:Condition interaction was my main research question. results.title: Creating & Applying Weights
results.content:
Title: Creating & Applying Weights
# Creating & Applying Weights. ## About Creating and Applying Weights. Stats iQ allows users to apply weights so that if certain types of survey respondents are under or overrepresented, Stats iQ can be told that one row of data should count for more or less than a single response. To enable weights, your data must have a variable  that contains the desired weights. **Qtip**: You can also create a variable that contains your desired weights by exporting your data, adding the column, and reimporting (see the Import Responses page), however, we recommend using the **Create Variable** option when possible. ## Create a Weighting Variable. **Qtip:** Weighting variables are most helpful for users working out of imported data projects or those without access to the Weighting section of Data & Analysis. Any numerical variable from the dataset can be used as a weight, but in many cases, the necessary weights needed cannot be determined until after the data is collected. In this case a weighting variable must be manually created. The most common method for creating a weighted variable is to use the **Logic** option in the **Create Variable** menu (for more information on creating variables in Stats iQ, see the page on Variable Creation). ## Apply a Weighting Variable to the Dataset. Once a weighting variable exists in the dataset, the weights from this variable can be applied using the **Weighting** dropdown in the **Analysis Settings** menu. **Qtip:** “Qualtrics-defined weighting” is any weighting set up in the Weighting section of the Data & Analysis Tab. By default, weights will apply to all cards that are created after the weighting variable is selected in **Analysis Settings**. In the Weighting section of Data & Analysis, weights are calculated automatically after the desired percentages of respondents are specified. In Stats iQ, weights must be determined manually before a weighting variable can be created. This allows for many more options in terms of how variables are applied, but requires an understanding of how to calculate weights. The values of the weighting variable would be 0.83 and 1.25 for respondents with and without children, respectively.
